activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, usually on April 4 or 5, families visit their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings.
story:
On the first Saturday of April, William found his grandmother on the back porch with a plastic bag full of small brooms, cloths, and paper money folded into intricate gold shapes. He knew exactly what the bag was for, because Grandpa had explained it last spring, before he got sick.

In the flashback that played in William's mind, he was nine, sitting on this same porch while Grandpa folded the same kind of gold paper. "Next April," Grandpa had said, "I'll take you to my father's grave. It's called Qingming, the tomb-sweeping festival. It usually falls on April 4 or 5. Families visit their ancestors' graves, clean them, and leave offerings." Grandpa had laughed and added, "Your uncle Seamus once swept the wrong headstone and left a whole plate of oranges on a stranger's grave." William had laughed too, and promised he would come.

Now Grandpa was the one being visited. William had worked out a problem on his own: which day should they go? His birthday was April 3, but a festival was not a birthday. He checked the calendar and found that Qingming fell on April 5 this year, so he circled it in red and showed his grandmother. "You figured that out yourself," she said, and she allocated the sweeping to him, the polishing of the stone to herself, and the carrying of offerings to Uncle Seamus and his son Lukas, who was William's age.

On the morning of April 5, they drove to the cemetery. Grandpa's stone had a thin layer of winter grime. William swept it in careful strokes, the way Grandpa had once swept his own father's stone, top to bottom, left to right. Lukas wiped the carved letters until they shone. They set out oranges, the gold paper shapes, and Grandpa's favorite sesame candies.

Then Uncle Seamus told the wrong-headstone story, and Lukas laughed so hard he had to sit down on the grass. William put one last orange on the stone, exactly in the center, and said, "We'll come back next April, Grandpa. I'll bring the broom."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The 2003 book "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players.
story:
The group chat pinged at 7:04 with the same message it got every Friday: "Court at the park, 3pm, first to five wins respect." Hayden had come to think of the message as a ritual, almost sacred to his friend Ann, who sent it with the seriousness of a royal proclamation. The problem was that "respect" always went to whoever scored the flashiest basket, and Hayden, who was not flashy, kept ending up picked last even though his team usually won when he played.

That Sunday his uncle had dragged him to a sports bar to watch baseball, and between innings the uncle leaned over his nachos and said, "You know the 2003 book Moneyball, by Michael Lewis? It described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used a statistic like on-base percentage to find undervalued players." Hayden had nodded, but the words stuck to him like gum to a shoe. Undervalued. That word was about him, possibly, although it also might just mean "bad at basketball," so he decided to test it.

The test was simple in idea and tedious in practice. He made a chart on graph paper and, for two weeks, tracked every pickup game in the chat: who was on which team, who touched the ball before a score, who got back on defense. Logging it felt like counting ants in a sidewalk crack. But a pattern grew in the numbers, quiet and stubborn, like mold in a lunchbox. Whenever Hayden played, his teams won more, even though he scored the least.

On Friday he posted the chart to the chat, with a caption: "New captain selection system, based on real data, not on Ivana doing one behind-the-back dribble last June." Ivana replied with seventeen angry-face emojis and then, three minutes later, "wait, run it again with me included properly."

Saturday, the picker chose Hayden first, and Ivana's team lost 5-2, which everyone agreed proved nothing at all, since Ann had spent the whole game guarding the wrong basket. "Statistics," Hayden announced solemnly, "never lie, but they do nap sometimes." Ann threw the ball at his head.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: Many shelf labels show a unit price, such as the price per litre, so different sizes can be compared; the bigger carton is often, but not always, cheaper per litre.
story:
The note in his hand said: 2 litres of milk, exact change, walk fast. Harrison had read it four times before he even reached the corner store, because this was his first solo mission and he wanted zero mistakes. His mother's coins rattled in his pocket like tiny applause.

Inside, the dairy case was colder than a snowbank, and the shelves hummed. He grabbed a big two-litre carton, then noticed a yellow sticker beside the price, tiny print reading price per litre. Two one-litre cartons sat nearby. He did quick math with his lips moving, then checked the small print again. Two one-litres together cost less per litre than the single big carton. "Whoa," he said out loud. "The big one isn't always cheaper." He set the big carton down and picked up the two small ones, feeling like he'd cracked a secret code nobody else had noticed.

His classmate Cameron was already at the freezer, hunting the tropical popsicles, which were sold out, as usual. Cameron wanted orange-pineapple so badly he'd walked here in the rain yesterday, and today he was hunting again. "It's like a parasite," Cameron groaned, patting the empty shelf. "This store feeds on my hope." Harrison held up his two small cartons as evidence and said the bigger one wasn't always cheaper per litre, and Cameron said that refutes everything his big brother had ever told him about bulk buying, and he changed his mind about the giant juice jug he'd been carrying around, putting it back with a dramatic sigh.

At the till, Harrison counted his coins one by one, sliding them across the counter, then counted his change back into his palm, twice, the coins cool and jingling. The cashier waited without rushing him, which he appreciated. Outside, the streetlights were just flickering on. He ran the whole way home with the milk sacks swinging, and burst through the door shouting, "Change counted! Two litres! And guess what isn't always cheaper?"

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Washington's Zackery Lystedt Law, passed in 2009, was the first U.S. state law requiring that a young athlete with a suspected concussion be removed from play until a health professional clears them.
story:
Mackenzie crouched at the starting line of the school track, laces double-knotted, eyes on the orange cones ahead. Tryouts for the spring team were one afternoon only, and she had been waiting all winter. Before the sprints began, she watched Stanley, who was a proud carnivore and always chewing beef jerky at lunch, jog the warm-up lap like it was nothing. Then he tripped over the inside rail, tumbled onto the rubber, and sat up slowly, blinking.

"I'm fine," Stanley said, waving off the coach. "I can't skip the hurdles. This is my only shot."

Mackenzie had noticed something, though. He was squinting at the scoreboard as if the numbers were swimming. She began to hypothesize: if he had hit his head hard enough to scramble his vision for even a minute, then something was wrong that she couldn't see, and there might be a rule about exactly that. She remembered a poster in her dentist's office, of all places.

"Stanley, wait," she said, jogging over. "There's a law. Washington's Zackery Lystedt Law, passed in 2009. It was the first state law in the country that says a young athlete with a suspected concussion has to come out of play until a health professional clears them."

Stanley stared at her. "That's a real law?"

"First of its kind in the whole U.S.," said Alizee, who was stretching on the next lane and had overheard. "My cousin sat out two weeks because of it."

The coach, an eccentric man who wore a whistle on a beaded chain and a different pair of mismatched socks every day, nodded. "She's right. You're done for today, Stanley. Doc clears you, you get another tryout."

Stanley's shoulders dropped, and Mackenzie thought he might argue. Instead he rubbed the back of his head and said quietly, "Okay. I'd rather sit out one day than the whole season." He walked to the bench and pulled out his jerky.

Mackenzie toed the line again, heart drumming. The starter raised the flag, and she ran.

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: A battery turns stored chemical energy into electrical energy, and it goes flat when those chemicals are used up.
story:
Nevaeh sat cross-legged on the garage floor beside the workbench, holding the circuit she had built yesterday: a battery, a switch, and a small bulb joined with copper wire. She flipped the switch. Nothing happened. The bulb stayed dark, and that was a problem, because her objective was to demonstrate the circuit to Ms. Rosen's science class tomorrow morning.

She checked the wires first. Each one was still clipped tight, and the switch clicked when she moved it, so the metal parts were touching. She unhooked the bulb and touched its bottom to the battery terminal directly, the way she had tested it before. Still dark.

Joelle came through the side door with her bike helmet still on. "Did you break it?"

"I don't think so." Nevaeh turned the battery over in her hand. It was the same battery from yesterday, when the bulb had glowed bright enough to read by. "Everything looks right. Same wires, same bulb, same switch."

"Then the missing piece is something we can't see," Joelle said. She pointed at the battery. "Maybe it's that."

Nevaeh thought about it. A battery turns stored chemical energy into electrical energy. She said the words out loud, and then the rest came: if those chemicals got used up, there would be nothing left to turn into electricity, even if every wire was perfect. That would explain why it worked yesterday and stayed dark today. It also gave her a test. She found a fresh battery in the drawer, swapped it in, and closed the switch.

The bulb lit, a small luminous circle on the concrete floor.

"Told you," Joelle said. "It went flat."

"The chemicals ran out," Nevaeh said. "A battery only sustains the circuit until they're gone. Then you need a new one." She put the flat battery in her pocket so she could show the class both sides of it, the dark one and the glowing one, and flipped the switch off and on twice just to watch it light again.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: An anecdote is a story about one person's experience; it cannot show that one thing caused another, because other explanations for what happened have not been ruled out.
story:
Autumn raised her hand so fast her chair squeaked. "Ms. Nwosu, my cousin swears her lucky pencil is why she passed her math test. Could we test that?" She had been wondering about it all weekend, ever since her uncle held up his copper bracelet at dinner and declared it had cured his back pain. Nobody had argued with him. Autumn hadn't either, but a question had been tickling her ever since: how would anyone know?

"Design an experiment," said Ms. Nwosu. "Show me your plan first."

At the lab table, Rosalyn flipped through her notebook. "We could have people take a quiz with the lucky pencil and a regular pencil and compare scores."

"But it's not really her pencil," Autumn said. "It's just a pencil we call lucky. That's the part I want to figure out. When my uncle says the bracelet fixed his back, he's telling a story about himself. Marlee told me there's a word for that."

"An anecdote," Marlee said, popping the cap off a marker. "A story about one person's experience. It can't show that one thing caused another, because other explanations haven't been ruled out."

"Like what?" Rosalyn asked.

"Like his back might have gotten better anyway," Autumn said slowly, drawing two boxes in her margin. "Or he started sleeping differently. Or he just believed it would work." The thought felt like a small revolution in her head, everything turning to face a new direction. One story was not the same as evidence, and the difference between them was suddenly distinct and obvious, like two separate doors she had been treating as one.

They ran the test the next day. Ten classmates took the same ten vocabulary questions twice, once with the "lucky" pencil and once with an ordinary one, with the order flipped for half of them. The scores were almost identical, and the two kids who did better with the lucky pencil had done the easy questions that round.

"Order," Rosalyn groaned, highlighting the pattern in yellow. "The second set was easier for them. That's the other explanation."

"So one person's story can't prove it," Autumn said, "because of stuff exactly like this, hiding in the background." She taped their chart to the whiteboard and stood back. "I'm going to tell my uncle we need thirty uncles and two bracelets."

activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: Bright screens late at night can delay sleep, because light, especially blue light, signals the brain to hold back the sleep hormone melatonin.
story:
Mason had never slept over anywhere but his own house, so when his cousin Winter invited him and Chaya for the night, he packed his bag like the weekend might last a month. Winter's house had a basement with a couch, a bowl of popcorn the size of a mixing vessel, and a tablet propped against a stack of board games. They watched video after video until Winter's mom called down that it was eleven o'clock and lights out meant lights out.

The lights went out, and then nothing happened. Mason lay on the air mattress listening to Chaya flip her pillow for the fourth time. "I'm so tired," she whispered, "but my brain won't shut off." Winter groaned from the couch. Mason stared at the ceiling and thought about the order of the evening. The videos had preceded the dark by hours, but his eyes still felt bright, like the screen was still glowing behind them. He sat up.

"Wait," he said. "My grandpa does this thing where he stops looking at his phone an hour before bed. He says the light, especially the blue light, tells your brain to hold back the sleep hormone."

"The sleep what?" Chaya asked.

"Melatonin," Mason said. "That's what he calls it. Bright screens late at night delay sleep because the light signals your brain to hold back melatonin."

"So we basically bathed our eyeballs in blue light for three hours," Winter said, "and now we can't sleep. Great. Science is ruining my life."

Mason found his flashlight in his bag and kept it pointed at the floor, dim and low. "We can't undo it. But maybe we can test it. No screens, no bright lights, just boring dark, and we see who falls asleep first." Chaya suggested they whisper stories instead of watching anything, and the yawning started almost immediately. When Chaya yawned, Mason yawned, and Winter accused them both of making it contagious on purpose.

Before he finally drifted off, Mason wrote a note on the back of a popcorn-stained receipt and left it on the tablet so morning-Winter would find it. "Dear future us: screens make the brain hold back melatonin, which is why we were awake until forever. Turn the tablet off by ten tomorrow. Signed, the scientist on the air mattress." In the morning, Winter held the note up and read it out loud at breakfast, and for once he didn't make fun of anything. "Same time next month," he said, sliding the tablet into a drawer, "but the videos end at nine."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs, so they should never be given as treats.
story:
Camille set the puppy's crate by the couch, where she could see it from the kitchen. The puppy, a small brown mutt her mom had finally agreed to, watched her every move. She had a list of first-day rules taped to the fridge, and at the top she had written, "Feeding," because feeding seemed like the most important thing a person could get right.

That afternoon Kaleigh came over with a bag of trail mix to celebrate. They sat on the porch floor and let the puppy tumble between them. Camille loves this, she thought, and reached into the bag for a handful of raisins to share. Kaleigh grabbed her wrist. "Wait, you can't. Raisins can hurt dogs. It's their kidneys. Grapes too, so grapes and raisins should never be given as treats." Camille stared at the small wrinkled fruits in her palm. She had been about to hand them over like they were ordinary dog food.

Camille wanted proof, though, because Kaleigh got things wrong sometimes. She texted Kole, whose family had two dogs, and he answered right away: "Never. Not even one. My vet has a poster about it." Then Camille checked the animal hospital's website, part of the big network of vet pages her mom had bookmarked the day they picked the puppy up. Every page said the same thing. She closed her fist around the raisins and carried them back inside to the counter, far from the puppy's reach.

"I was this close," Camille said, holding up two fingers nearly touching. "I thought fruit meant healthy. For everybody."

"For humans," Kaleigh said. "Dogs get their own rules."

Camille wrote a new line at the top of the fridge list and underlined it twice. The puppy bumped her shin with its nose, and she knelt down and offered it a piece of plain kibble instead.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Most food chains start with the sun, because plants and algae, the producers, use sunlight to make their own food by photosynthesis.
story:
Elijah stood at the pond exhibit in the science museum, staring at a glass tank full of green water. Rex was already scribbling on the worksheet: frog, snake, hawk, done.

"Your chain starts with a frog," Elijah said. "Where does the frog get its energy?"

"From whatever it eats," Rex said. "Bugs."

"Right. And bugs eat... what, exactly?"

Rex tapped his pencil against the glass. "Stuff. Leaves, maybe?"

Kaia leaned in between them, pointing at a sign near the tank. "Algae. Look, it says algae are producers. That means they make their own food."

Elijah frowned at the tank, at the cloud of green drifting under the surface. "Make it out of what? There's no kitchen in there."

"Sunlight," Kaia said. "The sign says most food chains start with the sun, because plants and algae, the producers, use sunlight to make their own food by photosynthesis."

Elijah wrote SUN in big letters at the top of his page, then algae, then bug, frog, snake, hawk. It looked strange, having the sun in a food chain, like putting a lamp on a menu. But the more he thought about it, the more it made sense. The hawk traced back to the snake, the snake to the frog, the frog to the bugs, the bugs to the algae, and the algae to sunlight hitting the water. Nothing started from nowhere.

Mr. Traoré appeared behind them with his hands in his pockets. "Nice work. Now here's the controversial question of the day. Suppose all the frogs vanish. What happens to your chain?"

Rex shrugged. "Fewer frogs. The end."

"No, wait," Elijah said. He covered the word FROG with his thumb and studied what was left. "The snakes lose their food, so they get hungry and move somewhere else. And the bugs go crazy, because nothing is eating them anymore. They'd eat all the algae."

"So the water changes," Kaia said slowly.

Elijah grabbed a fresh worksheet and started again, this time drawing arrows backward from the hawk down to the sun. He wanted to test the idea, to see if one missing link really could pull the whole chain apart from both directions at once. When he finished, he held the page up beside Rex's.

"Same chain," Elijah said. "But now we can see the whole thing, starting with the sun."

Rex looked at both pages, then grinned and erased his first attempt. "Okay. Sun first. No monopoly on good ideas, though, that was all you."

Mr. Traoré tapped Elijah's drawing with one finger. "That one goes on the wall by the tank."

Elijah followed him to the exhibit board, worksheet held out flat so the sun at the top wouldn't bend.

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
knowledge_domain: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
fact: Anxiety disorders are treatable, and cognitive behavioral therapy, which teaches people to notice and change anxious thoughts, is one of the most effective treatments.
story:
The note was folded into a tiny square and stuck under Piper's toothbrush in the camp bathroom. Camp Pinesong had a rule that the whole week seemed to revolve around: the buddy system, the whistle system, the check-in board where every camper moved a clothespin from "cabin" to "beach." But nobody had a system for notes in the bathroom. Piper unfolded it by the sinks and read: "I can't do the swim test tomorrow. Don't tell anyone. Dev."

At breakfast, Piper watched Dev across the picnic table. Dev hadn't touched his pancakes, though yesterday he'd eaten three. He kept his hood up even though it was already hot, and when Tommy joked about the giant rodent someone had spotted behind the mess hall, Dev didn't even smile. His knee bounced under the table, quick and constant, like a small engine. Piper thought about last summer, when her cousin had stopped eating and stopped sleeping and everyone had said "she's just shy" until it got so bad she couldn't go to school at all. Piper had been ten then and had told nobody. She still turned that over sometimes, wondering if speaking up would have made her cousin better sooner, or just made her mad.

The note said don't tell anyone. But Piper had a theory that "anyone" wasn't the same as "an adult whose whole job is campers." At craft hour she tested it, casually, sliding onto the bench beside Mr. Popal, the water-safety counselor who ran the lake. "Hypothetically," she said, "if someone wasn't eating and couldn't sleep and was scared of the swim test, would telling you count as telling anyone?" Mr. Popal set down his whistle. "Hypothetically," he said, "that's called noticing warning signs, and I'd want to know."

That evening Dev sat with her on the dock, feet dangling over the black water. "Mr. Popal talked to me," he said. "I was mad for about an hour." Then he shrugged. "Last year I saw a counselor for anxiety. It's treatable, that's the first thing she told me. We did cognitive behavioral therapy." He picked at a splinter. "It teaches you to notice anxious thoughts and change them. She said it's one of the most effective treatments there is." He grinned sideways. "So the twist is, I already know the swim test can't actually drown me. I just forgot for a week."

The next morning Dev moved his clothespin to "beach" without being asked, and Piper stood beside him at the lake's edge while Mr. Popal buckled his life vest. "Ready?" Mr. Popal called. Dev took a breath, and Piper cupped her hands around her mouth. "Noticing!" she shouted, and Dev laughed, and dove in.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Muslims perform the ritual prayer, salah, five times a day, facing the Kaaba in Mecca.
story:
Stella stood at the edge of the community hall with a plastic cup of juice in her hand and a problem in her head. She had told Kohen and Karlee she was fasting until sundown like her family did during Ramadan, and she had lasted through lunch, through the smell of the bake sale table, through Karlee eating a cookie right in front of her. That part was hard but simple. The confusing part came when her grandmother texted: pray at four, like we do.

Four o'clock found her in the hallway by the coat racks, holding her phone. Kohen was there, retying his sneaker. "What are you doing?" he asked.

"Trying to figure out which way to pray," Stella said. "My grandma says we face toward Mecca. But which way is that from here?" She turned in a slow circle. The hallway looked the same in every direction, water fountain, bulletin board, doors.

Kohen got up. "My uncle prays five times a day. He has an app." He pulled out his phone and tapped at it, then held the screen flat like a tiny tray. A green arrow appeared. "It's called salah," he said. "The prayer. It points to the Kaaba, in Mecca." He turned slowly until the arrow lined up with the far wall. "That way. Northeast, sort of."

Stella frowned at her own phone. She had been about to guess. Guessing the direction seemed like the kind of thing you could get wrong for years and never notice, because nothing would tell you. There was no mark left behind if you faced the wrong wall. She opened the compass app and watched the needle settle, then compared it to Kohen's arrow. They matched.

"It's the same for everybody, isn't it," she said. "Five times a day, from anywhere, everyone facing the same place."

"From what I've seen, yeah," Kohen said.

She set her juice on the windowsill. The hall thermostat on the wall read twenty-two degrees, and outside it was hot enough that Karlee had winced stepping off the bus. Stella found a clear patch of floor near the coat racks, laid her jacket down, and stood facing the direction the two arrows agreed on.

Karlee appeared in the doorway. "You're not drinking your juice?"

"Not until the sun goes down," Stella said. "Four o'clock is prayer time first." She stood still, facing northeast, and began.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Saying 'I'm sorry if you were upset' is often called a non-apology, because it expresses regret about the other person's feelings rather than about what the speaker did.
story:
Mila found Odalys on the bench by the estuary, where the river widened and slowed before it met the sea. The air was humid and heavy, and Odalys was reading Mila's text out loud to Charles in a voice like a judge announcing a verdict. "'Sorry if you got upset about Saturday.'" Odalys looked up. "That's not sorry for anything. That's sorry I got upset, like it's my fault for having feelings."

"It's a non-apology," Charles said, kicking at the gravel. "My sister calls them that. You're apologizing for my feelings instead of for what you did." He shrugged, as if to say he was only the messenger.

Mila opened her mouth to argue and then closed it. She had missed Saturday because her grandmother's visit got moved, and instead of saying so, she had typed that sentence fast, wanting the whole thing to be over. She tested the idea in her head, turning it like a coin: if she crossed out the word "if," what would be left? "Sorry you got upset about Saturday." Still Odalys's feelings. She would have to name what she herself had done. She thought back to three weeks ago, when Odalys had forgotten Mila's birthday picnic in this same park and shown up an hour late with a burnt cake, and Mila had said it was fine. She had nurtured that small hurt quietly, feeding it every time Odalys talked too long about other friends, until it had grown into not answering texts. Maybe the text hadn't started the fight at all. Maybe it only uncovered it.

"I did a bad thing," Mila said. "Not Saturday, exactly. When you were late to my picnic, I said it was fine and it wasn't, and I've been keeping score ever since. I'm sorry I did that." Odalys blinked, then held up her phone. "Then I'm sorry I read your text out loud to Charles like a court exhibit." Charles groaned. "Can I be sorry I had to hear both of you?" Odalys laughed first, then Mila, and then Odalys pulled two melted chocolate bars out of her bag and held one out across the humid air. Mila took it.

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: When two singers hold nearly but not exactly the same pitch, the sound pulses with a wobble called beats, which slows and disappears as they match.
story:
Sunlight through the stained glass window refracted into little pools of red and blue on the carpet, and Autumn stared at one of them instead of at her sheet music, because the music was not the problem. The problem was Izaiah. They were both altos, and the choir performed in three days, and every time they landed on the same long note, something in the sound went wrong in a way she could not point to.

"Hold the F," said Ms. Khan, tapping the piano. "Just the two altos. Everyone else, rest."

They sang. The note started clean, then it began to shudder, swelling and shrinking, like a moth beating against a jar. Autumn stopped. Izaiah stopped. The pools of colored light sat there being innocent.

"That pulsing," Autumn said. "It slows down when we get closer. Listen." She sang her F and slid hers slightly flat, and the wobble sped up. She slid back toward his pitch and the wobble stretched out, slower, slower, and then vanished entirely, and their two voices fused into one note so wide and warm that she felt it in her teeth.

"That's called beats," said Izaiah. "My cousin told me once."

"Then we don't listen for the right note," Autumn said, already flipping to the anthem. "We listen for the wobble to stop."

Ms. Khan had them run it again, and this time Autumn tracked the pulsing like following a string through a maze, easing her pitch until the sound smoothed out. On the last held note, the whole choir joined, and nothing wobbled anywhere.

Afterward Ms. Khan said it was the best the altos had ever sounded, which was, Autumn privately noted, not a high bar. She gathered her music, still hearing the shudder in her memory like something swallowed.

"Sunday," said Izaiah at the door. "Don't go larva on me. All curled up and lethargic in the back row."

"Sunday," said Autumn, "I will be the wobble-hunter."

He laughed so hard he dropped his folder, and she walked out through the red and blue pools toward the parking lot.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In a 1977 study, Lynn Hasher and colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true.
story:
Jack had exactly forty dollars and one hour before his mom picked him up at the food court entrance at five o'clock. The shoes he wanted, the silver-and-blue ones everybody at school talked about, cost sixty-five. He stood in front of the sports store window, watching a video loop play on the screen inside. A famous point guard sprinted across a court, then looked straight into the camera and said, "I never lace up anything else." Under him, flashing letters shouted MILLIONS AGREE. THE GREATEST GRIP EVER ENGINEERED.

"They're unbelievable," said Brycen, who had appeared beside him with a smoothie. "Legendary. Revolutionary."

"Those are just the ad's words," Jack said. "Loaded words. They don't tell you anything." But he said it without much conviction, because the weird thing was that the shoes did feel unbelievable to him now. He had heard they were the best five separate times today: once from Yousef, once from a kid in math class, twice from the video loop, once from a radio spot in the parking garage. Nobody had shown him a single test, a single number, and yet somewhere in his head the claim had hardened into fact.

He tried an experiment on himself. "Say 'the mall fountain grants wishes' five times," he told Brycen.

"Fine. The mall fountain grants wishes. The mall fountain grants wishes. The mall fountain..." Brycen counted on his fingers through all five, then frowned. "Okay, that actually felt true for a second. That's creepy."

They found Yousef near the fountain, wearing a T-shirt with a cartoon kangaroo on skates, some mascot from a defunct juice stand, and Jack told him about the experiment. Yousef nodded. "My sister read about that. In a 1977 study, Lynn Hasher and colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true."

"So the repetition is doing the persuading," Jack said slowly, "not the proof." He looked back at the window, at the point guard he'd never meet, at the word MILLIONS, at kids from the affluent side of town walking out with boxes. He checked his budget again. Forty dollars, no matter how many times he counted it.

"Foot Locker clearance rack is two stores down," Yousef said. "Forty-two bucks, and they grip fine."

Jack looked at the clock above the register. Four fifty-one. He jogged toward clearance, Brycen and Yousef right behind him, and pulled a plain gray pair off the bottom shelf. "Hold these till I get back," he called to the cashier, and sprinted for the food court door to intercept his mom and ask for two dollars.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, slurping noodles such as ramen and soba is considered acceptable at the table rather than rude.
story:
Isaac had been postponing his science worksheet all through lunch because the cafeteria looked different today. Ms. Sutherland had set up long tables diagonal to the windows for International Food Day, and families had brought dishes from home. Safiya, who had signed up three weeks early, was guarding her samosas like treasure, hoping people would try them before the pizza line emptied the room of customers. Isaac's real worry, though, was Marion.

Marion had invited him to her family's table, where her mother had set out a huge pot of ramen. Isaac took a bowl, thanked her, and then nearly dropped his chopsticks. Marion slurped. Not a small slurp either, but a long, loud, glorious one, noodles vanishing into the steam. Her mother slurped too. So did Marion's little brother, who was mostly missing his mouth.

Isaac glanced at Safiya, who raised an eyebrow as if to say, do something. Isaac quietly ate without making a sound, the way he'd been taught at his grandmother's table, and waited for an adult to say something polite and terrible. Nobody did. That was the strange part. When Marion's mother offered seconds, she smiled widest at the brother, whose slurp had been the loudest of all.

So Isaac tested it. He slurped his next mouthful of noodles, feeling his ears go hot. Marion's mother laughed warmly and refilled his bowl before he could say no thank you. "You slurp like my uncle in Osaka," Marion said. "In Japan, slurping noodles like ramen and soba is acceptable at the table. It isn't rude there at all." Isaac, mouth still full, could only nod.

Safiya arrived at the table with the last samosa on a napkin, having calculated that a fair percentage of the crowd had gone for ramen instead. "Trade?" she said, holding it out to Marion. "You got the popular dish." Marion split the samosa in half, and Isaac slurped another mouthful so loudly that the little brother stopped, stared, and offered a solemn high five across the table.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is browning that happens when sugar alone is heated, which makes it a different reaction from the Maillard reaction, which also needs amino acids.
story:
Blake stood in Grandpa's kitchen with a heavy pot and a bag of sugar, because tonight he was making caramel sauce for dessert, all by himself. His friend Dillon had come along, mostly to watch and eat. "Is this the same browning as the crust on Grandpa's roast?" Dillon asked, peering into the pot as Blake turned the burner on. Blake thought about it while he sprinkled in the sugar. The roast had browned too, but that had meat juices in it, and meat has protein. This pot had nothing but sugar. "It can't be the same," he said slowly. "There's nothing in here but sugar. It's just sugar alone being heated." Dillon shrugged and leaned on the counter.

Grandpa, who was fiddling with the thermostat because the old house ran cold, called over, "Careful, that melted sugar is volatile stuff. One minute pale, next minute burnt." Blake kept his eyes glued to the pot, whisk in hand. He decided to test his idea. If sugar alone browned, then the browning must happen without anything else in the pot, and he could watch it happen stage by stage. First the sugar melted and went clear. Then, slowly, it turned gold, then amber, then a deep copper. Nothing had been added the whole time. So this browning needed only heat and sugar.

"It's called caramelization," Blake announced, "browning that happens when sugar alone is heated." Dillon frowned. "Then what was the roast doing?" Blake remembered a word from a science video he'd half watched. "That's the Maillard reaction. It also needs amino acids, the stuff in meat. So they're two different reactions." He grabbed a notebook and wrote it down so he'd remember for the science fair. "Two brownings, two causes," he said, and did a small victory spin with the whisk.

Then the smoke alarm shrieked. Blake yanked the pot off the burner a second too late; the copper had gone dark and bitter. He stared at the ruined batch, shoulders dropping. Dillon tried to console him. "It's okay, man, it smelled amazing for a whole minute." Blake dumped the pot in the sink, set out a fresh bag of sugar, and pointed the whisk at the stove. "Round two. You watch the clock this time."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Research on children at overnight camps has found that most campers feel at least some homesickness during their stay, and for most of them it stays mild.
story:
The camp bus wouldn't reach Lake Wendell for another forty minutes, and Quentin had already asked the driver to stop three times. "I need to call my mom," he said, gripping the seat in front of him. "I forgot my allergy pills, and my prescription is at home, and I'm going back." The driver said they didn't turn around for forgotten pills, especially pills Quentin didn't actually take anymore.

Savannah, sitting across the aisle, had her own problem. She was the only one of her friends going to overnight camp, and she'd decided, somewhere around the highway on-ramp, that she was the only person on the bus who felt like her stomach had been swapped with a bag of rocks. She was also, in an impulsive way, a person who counted things. She had once tallied every red car in the school parking lot for a week. So she pulled a notebook out of her backpack and wrote a plan: before the bus arrived, she would ask every camper one question and find out for sure.

She started with Zaynab, two rows up. "On a scale of one to ten, how much do you miss home right now? Don't think about it, just say a number." Zaynab said six. The boy by the window said four. A girl with braided hair said seven and a half. Quentin said eleven, then asked if he could put his name in bold letters on the page. Savannah worked her way down the aisles, keeping her voice low so the driver wouldn't think she was causing trouble, and by the time the bus took the exit ramp she had twenty-eight numbers. Twenty-six of them were higher than one. Most were fours, fives and sixes.

Mr. Munro, the counselor riding up front, came back to collect the sick bags someone had scattered, and the notebook slid off Savannah's knee into the aisle. He picked it up, glanced at the column of numbers, and handed it back without a word, but tucked between the seats he'd dropped his staff binder, and a printed page stuck out of it. Savannah read the heading upside down, then right side up when she pulled it loose. Research on kids at overnight camps had found that most campers felt at least some homesickness during their stay, and for most of them it stayed mild. So her numbers weren't weird. They were normal, and normal meant survivable.

She tapped Quentin on the shoulder and turned the notebook toward him. "Twenty-six out of twenty-eight," she said. "You're not special. You're barely above average." Quentin stared at the column, then at the page from the binder, and let out a breath. "Fine," he said. "But if my mom asks, tell her I said ten." Through the windshield, a wooden sign shaped like a canoe came into view, and the whole bus leaned toward the glass to read it.

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
knowledge_domain: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
fact: Borrowing 100 dollars at 20 percent yearly interest and repaying it after one year costs about 20 dollars in interest, or more if interest compounds.
story:
Julia had been sweeping the front of Mr. García's bike shop every Saturday for a month, and every Saturday the green mountain bike in the window seemed to wink at her. It cost two hundred dollars. She had earned thirty-one dollars so far, plus nine from the lemonade stand she and Kellan had run in July.

"You should just ask your mom to put it on her credit card," Kellan said, leaning on the broom Julia was supposed to be using. "Then you'd have it today. I despise waiting, personally. Waiting is for suckers."

Julia stopped sweeping. "My mom says a credit card is borrowing money. You have to pay it back plus extra."

"That's the boring part. Skip the boring part."

That night, Julia got out a notebook and tested the idea, because Kellan's plan sounded great and her mom's face had not. If her mom borrowed one hundred dollars for her, and the card charged twenty percent interest for a year, then paying it back after one year would cost about twenty dollars extra. She wrote it out. One hundred dollars became one hundred twenty. Two hundred dollars became two hundred forty. And the receipt in her mom's drawer said "compounds," which her mom translated as: if you take longer, it costs more than that.

On Saturday, Julia marched into the shop. "Mr. García, if I borrow one hundred dollars from a credit card and pay it back after a year, it costs about twenty dollars in interest. More if it compounds."

Mr. García looked up from a wheel. "Sounds right. Why are you telling me my own business?"

"Because Kellan says I should do that for the green bike, and I worked it out, and borrowing two hundred dollars means paying back two hundred forty. That's like sweeping your floor for nothing for two whole months."

"Kellan has a monopoly on bad ideas," Mr. García said. "Nobody else can get a word in."

"He does. He's very proud of it."

Julia did the math another way. At her Saturday wages, she would have the bike by spring without owing anyone anything. Spring felt far away, but two hundred forty dollars felt worse. She taped a paper bicycle to her wall and colored in one wheel spoke every Saturday.

In March, Kellan was still paying his mom back for a video game he'd charged in December, plus extra, and he had gone quiet on the subject of suckers. Julia counted her jar one last time: two hundred and six dollars. She rode the green bike to the shop to show Mr. García, ringing the little bell twice, her rebellious ponytail escaping its elastic as she flew down the hill.

He came out and saluted. "Paid for with zero interest," he said.

"Zero," Julia said, and rang the bell again.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In French, à droite means to the right, while tout droit means straight ahead, a pair that often trips up learners asking for directions.
story:
"Excusez-moi, où est la pharmacie?" Violet asked the woman at the corner, gripping her clipboard. The woman smiled and answered in a rush of French, and Violet caught only two words: "tout droit." She turned to her group. "She said something about à droite. So we go right."

Alisha frowned at the photocopied map. "The pharmacy is on Rue Saint-Jean. That's straight past the bakery, isn't it?" Behind them, Leonie rubbed her arm where the travel clinic nurse had given her the vaccine that morning before the bus, and Violet's own arm gave a small ache of sympathy. They had fifteen minutes to buy the bandages Ms. Gagnon needed for their first-aid kit project, then meet the class at the fountain.

Violet looked at the map, then at the corner. The pharmacy symbol sat at the top of the page, straight up from where they stood. A street did branch off to the right, but nothing on the map was marked there. If the woman had meant right, the pharmacy should be on that side street. It wasn't. She exhaled slowly through her nose, the way she did before a difficult piano piece, and thought about the sounds. The woman had said "tout droit." Not just "à droite." Two different things, probably, because the woman had used both at some point, or had she? Violet closed her eyes and replayed the answer in her head. "Continuez tout droit." That was it. Continue. You continue when you keep going the way you already are.

"Wait," Violet said. "I think tout droit means straight ahead, and à droite means to the right. They sound almost the same, but she said tout droit, and she told us to continue. So we go straight." Alisha tilted her head. "You're sure?" "Testing it. If we walk two blocks straight and there's no pharmacy, we turn around." They walked past the bakery, where warm sugar and butter drifted out the open door, and past a bookshop with a cat sleeping in the window. At the second corner, the green cross of the pharmacy glowed above the door.

Inside, Violet asked the cashier for bandages in careful French, counted out the coins, and carried the small paper bag outside like a trophy. Leonie checked her watch. "Nine minutes to spare." They ran for the fountain, and when Ms. Gagnon raised an eyebrow at their flushed faces, Violet held up the bag and said, "On y est allées tout droit."

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: The darkest part of a cast shadow is right where the sphere touches the surface, because almost no light can reach into that narrow gap.
story:
Laurence squinted at her sketch pad and then at the ping-pong ball sitting on the art cabin's wooden table. Mr. Sokolov had set up the still life for everyone: one ball, one flashlight clipped to a shelf, one hour before the camp art show opened at four. Her sphere had a nice highlight on the top left and a soft shadow curving away from the light, but something was wrong, and she couldn't name it.

"It looks like it's hovering," said Vera, leaning over from the next stool. Vera's own page had a lopsided blob that she insisted was "abstract," though what she really wanted was for the judges to hang her drawing next to the canoe rack where everyone walked past. "Mine's hovering too, but on purpose. Yours looks like a magic trick gone wrong."

Emaan, on Laurence's other side, was already halfway done. He had smudged his gray pencil until his ball looked so real that Laurence reached out, half expecting her finger to touch it. "How did you do the bottom?" she asked him. Emaan shrugged and held up his pencil. "I just pressed really hard in one tiny spot. Right under the ball. Don't ask me why it works." He was busy trying to finish before the bell so he could get the good table at the campfire snack, and he'd promised to save Laurence a marshmallow if she made the deadline too.

Laurence bent down until her eye was level with the table. The flashlight didn't emit much light into the thin space where the ball touched the wood, she realized, so that little sliver of contact was where the shadow went almost black. Everywhere else, light crept in from the sides and made the shadow grayer. She picked up her softest pencil and pressed hard, darkening just the crescent where ball met table, leaving the rest of the cast shadow lighter. Then she drew a faint line around the sphere's equator, the halfway curve she'd learned about yesterday, to make the shading turn evenly.

Vera scooted her stool closer and whispered, "Can you show me the pressing thing? Mine's floating worse than a hot air balloon." Laurence demonstrated on the corner of Vera's page, and Vera copied it, tongue sticking out, then let out a whoop when her blob finally sat down on its imaginary table. "It's grounded! It has a home now!" A few kids laughed, and even Mr. Sokolov cracked a smile from the doorway.

At three fifty-eight, Laurence added one last approximate touch of gray beneath the black crescent, so the shadow would fade smoothly outward. The bell rang, and Emaan grabbed both their pages and jogged them to the display table, saving spots side by side. Laurence followed, wiping graphite off her fingers, and stood back to look. Her sphere rested on the table, heavy and real, no longer floating anywhere but exactly where she'd put it. "Marshmallow tax," Emaan said, and held out his hand.

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Multiplying the top and bottom of a fraction by the same number makes an equivalent fraction, so one quarter equals three twelfths.
story:
Laurence sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with a worksheet, a pencil, and a slice of pizza that was going cold while she glared at the first problem: one quarter plus one third. Her grandmother had already asked twice whether she wanted more cheese on it. Laurence had said no twice.

"You look like the worksheet insulted you," said Simona, who had come over because her own house had no pizza and also no grandmother who made mango smoothies.

"It did insult me. The denominators don't match. You can't add fourths and thirds, that's like adding cats and scissors."

Her grandmother slid a whole pizza onto the table and, without a word, cut a quarter out of it. Then she took that quarter piece, cut it into three skinny slices, and fanned them out. "Three twelfths," she said, and went back to her crossword.

Laurence stopped chewing. She counted the skinny slices, then the twelve slices they would make across a whole pizza. She pulled her plate closer and cut her own slice the same way, muttering as she worked, and began to document her results in the margin of the worksheet like a scientist who suspected something remarkable. One quarter, cut into three pieces, made three twelfths. She tried it with half the pizza, cut into three, and got three sixths, which was still a half, sitting there pretending to be new.

"It works if you multiply the top and the bottom by the same number," she told Simona, with an assertive tap of the pencil. "So one quarter is three twelfths, and one third is four twelfths, and now they're both twelfths and I can actually add them."

Simona looked at the pizza, which now had a grid of cuts across it like a prism throwing lines everywhere. "So the answer is seven twelfths?"

"Seven twelfths." Laurence wrote it down and boxed it, then ate the evidence.

Her grandmother penciled in one more word of the crossword and slid the smoothie across the table.

activity: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
knowledge_domain: to search the web with specific keywords and tell an ad from a real result
fact: In Google, the word OR between two search words must be typed in capital letters to find pages containing either word.
story:
Antoine had exactly forty minutes before the library closed and before the deadline for Mr. Ionescu's class project expired at midnight, which would not have been a problem if his printer at home had not chosen tonight to release a puff of vapor and die. So here he was at the public library, hunched over a computer between two friends, typing "cats or dogs best pets" into the search bar and getting pages about nothing useful at all.

"Try it again," said Reuben, leaning over his shoulder. "Maybe the internet is just being moody."

"The internet is always moody," said Masen. "It's like a cat. Which is sort of our topic, so that's poetic."

Antoine typed the search a second time and got the same pile of junk. Mixed in with the results were boxes shouting WIN A FREE PHONE and TOP 10 PET DEALS, which he was starting to recognize as ads rather than real results. He remembered the day Mr. Ionescu had shown the class a page covered in blinking boxes and asked them to raise a hand when they spotted the fake one. "You're learning to see the invisible," Mr. Ionescu had said, which at the time had sounded like something a wizard would say. Now Antoine squinted at the screen, skipped anything with a tiny "Sponsored" tag, and felt slightly like a detective.

"Wait," he said slowly. "The word OR is lowercase. What if that matters?" He highlighted the o, deleted it, and retyped it in capital letters. The page refreshed, and suddenly the results showed sites about cats and sites about dogs, pages containing either word, exactly what he'd wanted. "It works! OR has to be in capital letters, all caps, or it doesn't count."

Masen gasped like Antoine had discovered fire. "You just collaborated with the computer and won."

"I didn't collaborate with anything, I just yelled at it in capital letters," Antoine said, but he was grinning. He narrowed his keywords further, adding "behavior" and "care," and the junk results thinned out like fog on a cool morning. Reuben pointed at one box that claimed a puppy could be delivered in an hour. "Definitely an ad," Antoine said, scrolling past it. "Real results don't promise you a puppy like a pizza."

At 8:58, two minutes before closing, Antoine hit print. The librarian appeared at the desk holding his warm pages, and outside the air had turned humid and heavy, the kind of night that made his shirt stick to his back all the way to the bus stop. He slid the report into his backpack, zipped it, and turned to his friends.

"Tomorrow I'm teaching my dad this trick," he said. "He thinks the search engine is out to get him."

Reuben clapped him on the shoulder. "Tell him to fight back in capital letters."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, and the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10.
story:
Arthur had heard the story about the first big game so many times that he could almost see it, and that was the problem. Grandpa Joe told it every year at Mr. Mehta's watch party, which was the best party on the block because Mr. Mehta had the biggest television and made samosas by the trayful. Arthur sat on the floor between his friends Tayla and Everly, a plate balanced on his knees, waiting for the moment.

It came in the second quarter. "I remember the very first one," Grandpa Joe announced from the good armchair. "January 15, 1967. Packers against the Chiefs, and the Packers won it thirty-five to ten." He said it the way he always did, like he was setting down a stone.

Everly leaned toward Arthur and whispered, "He says that every year. Do you think he really remembers it? He would have been a kid." Arthur had wondered the same thing. Grandpa Joe's memories sometimes got mixed up, like the time he swore he'd shaken hands with a president at a county fair. Tayla shrugged. "You could just ask him stuff."

Arthur decided to test the story instead. His idea was simple: if Grandpa Joe truly watched that game, he would know details that a person couldn't fake, and if he only knew the numbers, the story might come from somewhere else. So during a commercial, Arthur asked, "Grandpa, where did you watch it? Who was there?"

Grandpa Joe's face changed, going soft and far away. "My father's living room. The furniture was sparse back then, just a couch and two chairs, and the whole building crammed in because half the street didn't have a set yet." He described his mother keeping score on a grocery bag, and how the paper tore and a neighbor taped it back together at halftime. "I kept that bag for years," he added. "Wish I hadn't lost it. That's a choice I regret."

Arthur listened with both ears. The numbers matched every year, but this was different. This had people in it, a torn grocery bag, a neighbor with tape. You couldn't replicate a memory like that by repeating it; you could only have it. From Arthur's perspective on the floor, looking up, Grandpa Joe suddenly seemed less like a teller of tales and more like a man holding pieces of a day almost nobody else remembered.

Tayla nudged him. "So? Real or not?"

"Real," Arthur said, and Grandpa Joe, who had heard the whole exchange, raised his cup toward him across the crowded room.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A message sent in a private chat can be screenshotted and shared by anyone who receives it, so a private message is only as private as the people who read it.
story:
Bennett slid into his usual seat on the school bus, third row from the back, and pulled out his phone before the doors had even hissed shut. Somewhere behind him, Lucca was laughing with a knot of eighth graders, and the sound of it made Bennett's stomach tighten. Yesterday, in what he thought was a private chat with a kid from math class, Bennett had typed some things about Lucca. He had called him bossy. He had said Lucca acted like he owned the group project. It had felt good to type, the way yelling into a pillow feels good. Now he was not so sure it had stayed between the two of them, because at lunch Lucca had sat at the far end of the table and said nothing to him at all.

He tested his idea the only way he could think of. He opened the chat and reread his own message. Then he checked the other group chat, the big one with half the grade in it, where memes and soccer scores saturated the feed every afternoon. Nothing about him. Nothing yet. But that did not prove anything, and he knew it, because Ms. Wong had once said something in class that stuck in his head: a private message is only as private as the people who read it. Anyone who received it could screenshot it and pass it along, and then it lived wherever they put it.

The bus jolted over the tracks near Aila's stop, and Aila grabbed the seat back as she climbed the steps. She dropped into the seat across the aisle from Bennett and studied him with her eyebrows up.

"You look like you saw a ghost," she said.

"Worse." He turned the phone face down on his knee. "I said something mean about Lucca in a chat I thought was just me and one other kid. And now Lucca's not talking to me, and I don't know if he saw it or if he's just mad about the project."

Aila frowned. "So you don't actually know the cause. That's the whole problem. You're guessing."

"Exactly. There's no way to check the guess." He rubbed his thumb along the edge of the phone case. "Unless I just ask him."

"That's not guessing anymore. That's a test."

The bus pulled up to the school. Bennett stood, then stopped in the aisle where Lucca was gathering his backpack. The eighth graders had gone quiet, and the driver's mirror showed everyone's faces at once, small and staring.

"Lucca. Did you see something I wrote?" Bennett asked.

Lucca held up his phone, and there it was, a screenshot, his own words in somebody else's chat. "Marcus sent it to the big group this morning."

Bennett looked at the image of his message sitting there where it was never meant to be. "I'm sorry," he said. "I should have said it to your face, or not at all."

Lucca studied him for a long second, then shrugged one shoulder. "Then say it to my face now."

"You're bossy about the project. Sometimes. That's all it was."

"Okay," Lucca said. "Now I actually heard it. Get off the bus, bossy is going to be late for homeroom."

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Shoveling heavy snow is hard work for the heart, so doctors advise taking breaks and lifting small loads rather than big shovelfuls.
story:
The snow had come down all night, and by morning school was cancelled. Aiden pulled on his boots and walked to the park, where the hills were already loud with kids on sleds. On the way, he passed the little house beside the park gate, where Ms. Friedman was shoveling her driveway. She was moving slowly, and she kept stopping, one mittened hand pressed against her side.

Aiden watched from the sidewalk for a minute. His father had said something once about snow and older people, something he couldn't quite remember. Standing there, he made an inference: the stopping wasn't laziness or cold. Heavy snow was hard on the heart, so the stopping must be a way of protecting it. If that was true, then the huge shovelfuls she was heaving were the problem, and small loads would fix it.

"You should let me take a turn," he said, "and take little scoops instead of big ones. And maybe rest between rows."

Ms. Friedman leaned on her shovel. "Small scoops?"

"Half a shovel at a time," Aiden said. "Doctors say take breaks and lift small loads, not big ones. That's what my dad told my grandpa." He wasn't sure his memory was authentic, but she looked at him as if it might be, so he picked up the spare shovel by her porch step.

They worked row by row down the driveway. He shoveled one row while she stood by the gate catching her breath, and then she did the next while he rested and watched the sleds go flying down the park hill. The work went slower than one person digging fast, but by the time they reached the sidewalk she was breathing easy and laughing at something he'd said about the snowman in the park, which wore an actual necktie.

Braeden and Lyanna came trudging past with a sled between them. "Come to the hill," Braiden called. "Best snow all winter."

Aiden looked at the clear driveway, then at the hill.

"Race you," he said, and grabbed his shovel.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: In a fair test, every other condition is kept the same, so any difference in results can be traced to the one variable that was changed.
story:
Joshua set the two bean pots side by side on the folding table in the gymnasium, smoothing his display board with the heel of his hand so the title stood straight: "Do Beans Grow Better With Music?" The gym smelled like floor wax and masking tape, and the bleachers rattled as other kids dragged in their tables. His left pot, the music pot, had grown tall and pale. His right pot, the silent one, was squat and dark green. On paper it looked like a discovery, the kind of thing people called a scientific frontier, a whole new question nobody had answered yet.

"Wow," said Ameera, leaning over his table. "The music one totally won."

Joshua grinned, but then he stopped. Something about the tall, pale plant bothered him. Pale meant reaching for something, the way plants reached for light. He closed his eyes and tried to picture his bedroom, where he had kept the pots for three weeks. He could almost smell the dusty windowsill, could almost hear the radio humming on the shelf beside it.

Then the flashback hit him whole. His dad carrying the pots upstairs, setting one pot on the sunny windowsill because it fit there, and the other on the dresser across the room because it didn't. The impulsive decision had taken ten seconds. "No, no, no," Joshua said out loud. He had not only played music for one pot. He had also given it the window.

"It's ruined," he said, and his voice cracked a little. "Both things changed. I can't interpret the results at all. Music, light, I don't know which one made the difference."

Ameera frowned at the pots. "So what do you do now?"

Ms. Mwangi passed by with a roll of tape, and Joshua caught her sleeve. "Ms. Mwangi, if I start over, how do I make it right?"

"You keep every other condition the same," she said, already walking on. "Then any difference in results can be traced to the one variable you changed."

Joshua grabbed a marker and wrote across the top of his board: ROUND TWO. Ameera laughed and pulled up a chair.

"New pots," Joshua said, already counting seeds out of the packet into his palm. "Same soil, same water, same shelf. This time the radio is the only thing that's different."

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In the United States, a bill must pass both the House of Representatives and the Senate in identical form before it goes to the president.
story:
The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and coffee, and the line of voters snaked between the basketball hoops. Chloe stood near the check-in table with her poster rolled under one arm, waiting for her mother to finish her ballot. Tomorrow she had to give a report in Mr. Santos-Reyes's class, and tonight the school was letting students set up civics displays at the polling station. She had picked the topic herself, how a bill becomes a law, and now she wasn't sure she actually understood it.

Jesse jogged over from the juice table, waving a folded newspaper. "Look at this. There are two versions of that park bill. One says the Senate passed it, one says the House passed it. Which one becomes the law?"

Chloe took the paper. Both articles were real, both votes had happened, and the two versions weren't even worded the same. She felt a hot flicker of panic, the same one she'd felt when she'd skipped the reading last week and guessed wrong on the quiz. She had guessed then. She didn't want to guess again.

"Okay," she said slowly. "Watch this." She unrolled her poster on the folding table and drew a quick sketch: two boxes labeled House and Senate, arrows, and a small figure at the end. "I think it's like this. The House passes its version. The Senate passes its version. But if they're not identical, it can't just move on." She traced the arrows with her marker. "It has to pass both, in the same form, before it goes to the president."

Chace, who had drifted over with a cookie, squinted at the drawing. "So in the news, neither one is the law yet?"

"That's my idea," Chloe said. "Let's test it." She walked to the check-in table, where Mr. Santos-Reyes was meticulously handing each voter the correct ballot for their residence, checking addresses line by line. "Mr. Santos-Reyes, quick question, not about voting. If a bill passes the House one way and the Senate another way, is it a law?"

He smiled and held up his hand like a stop sign. "I'm not telling you. That's your report, Chloe. But ask yourself: would you sign two papers that didn't say the same thing?"

She stood there a second. Then it landed, and she almost laughed. Of course. You wouldn't sign two different papers. The bill had to be identical in both places first, and only then did it reach the president's desk. It was a rule you couldn't see, but you could feel its shape, the way you could feel that the line of voters was moving even with your back turned.

Back at the table, she redrew her poster with the two boxes joined by a loop labeled "must match," then the arrow to the president. "Jesse, get your notebook and recount the steps out loud while I write them," she said, capping her marker. Chace read the headline one more time, then flipped the newspaper over. "So that park bill still has a long way to go," he said, and Chloe nodded, already printing the last word in careful block letters.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book 'Continuing Bonds' argued that keeping a connection to someone who has died, through memories, objects or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving.
story:
Connor found the watch in the cupholder, where Grandpa always left it during long drives. The leather band was warm from the sun, and the second hand still ticked, even though the funeral had been three days ago and Grandpa had been gone two weeks before that. Connor slipped it on his wrist. It was too big, so he made a fist to keep it from sliding off.

"Do you think that's weird?" he asked. His mom kept her eyes on the road, so Connor turned to Drayden in the back seat instead. They were driving to Grandpa's house to help sort his things, and Drayden had come along because Connor hadn't wanted to make the trip alone. "Wearing it. Drayden, I'm asking you. Does it mean I'm not moving on?"

Drayden pulled out his phone. "My counselor had this book on her shelf. It's called Continuing Bonds. Came out in 1996." He scrolled, then held the screen up. "It says keeping a connection to somebody who died, through memories or objects or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving. It's actually a whole idea people study."

Connor looked at the window. The fields outside were barren this time of year, brown and flat, and for a second he felt like that too, like nothing would grow in him again. Then he thought about how Grandpa used to orbit the kitchen every morning, coffee cup in one hand, checking the window for birds. Connor had always thought that was silly. Now he wasn't sure. Maybe he would start checking the window himself.

"Traditions," he said slowly. "Like the drive to get donuts on Saturdays. Grandpa never skipped it. Not once."

"So don't skip it either," Drayden said. "That's not being stuck. That's the watch still ticking."

The jury in Connor's head had been out all week, and it wasn't back yet, but his fist loosened anyway. He rotated the watch until its face caught the light, then looked out at the birds following the car down the fence line. "Saturday," he said. "You're coming with me."

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: The ancient Egyptian pyramids were built as tombs for pharaohs, meant to protect the king's body and belongings for his life after death.
story:
Camille spread her poster board across the library table and frowned at the empty space in the middle. Her report was due Thursday, and she still could not answer the question Mr. Villanueva had written on the board: Why did the ancient Egyptians build the pyramids, and how did the Nile shape their farming? She had a stack of books, a plastic tub of sand Angad had carried in from the art room, and a half-inch of water in a squeeze bottle. Anais dropped into the chair across from her and peered at the sand.

"What's the tub for?" Anais asked.

"Testing," Camille said. She had read that the Nile flooded every year, and she wanted to see what that would do to farmland. She tilted the tub so the sand piled at one end, then pressed a shallow channel down the middle with her finger. "This part is the river. These flat bits are fields." She squeezed water slowly into the channel until it crept over the edges and darkened the sand on both sides. When the water soaked in, she lifted the tub to eye level to magnify the view of the thin layer of wet silt left behind, and the pattern made sense at once. The flood was not a disaster. It was delivery. Wet mud, spread across the fields, year after year.

"Okay, that's farming," said Angad, sliding a book toward her. "Now look at this." It was a cutaway picture of a pyramid, sliced open like a cake. Deep inside, near the middle, was a small room with a stone chest in it. Angad tapped the room. "I thought pyramids were palaces. Like, the pharaoh lived in the top and looked out."

Camille studied the picture. "If it were a palace, where are the windows? The kitchens? There's just this little room buried in all that stone." She turned pages until she found the caption, and read it twice to be sure. "It's a burial chamber. The whole pyramid is a tomb, built to protect the pharaoh's body and his belongings for his life after death." That explained everything else, she realized. The treasure, the narrow passages, the sealed entrances. Nobody seals a palace like a vault.

"Mr. Villanueva?" Camille called softly, and the librarian came over. "Can I check out this model kit? It has a Nile with a little valve you open to flood the fields." He found the box and set it beside her sand tub.

"For the presentation?" he asked.

"Both," Camille said. She copied the cutaway picture onto her poster, drew arrows from the river to the fields, and wrote her answer at the top in careful letters: floods fed the fields, and the pyramids kept the pharaoh safe for the life after this one. Anais read it over her shoulder and nodded.

"One more thing," Angad said, pointing at a drawing of birds in the corner of a page. "The Egyptians watched these migratory birds arrive every year right before the flood. The birds were like a warning sign."

Camille added one bird to her river, wings spread, flying north. Then she squeezed the bottle again and watched the water rise.

activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
knowledge_domain: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
fact: Most plant cells lack centrioles, small structures animal cells use when they divide.
story:
Charles had a science worksheet due Monday, a chart comparing a plant cell and an animal cell, and no desk he wanted to sit at on a Saturday. So he brought the worksheet to the community garden, where he was supposed to be helping his neighbor Ms. Khoury repair her dilapidated tomato cages.

"You're drawing instead of weeding," Ms. Khoury observed.

"I'm multitasking." He held up the paper. "Plant cell. I copied it off the board. Animal cell, too."

Alycia and Martin wandered over from the lettuce beds to look. Alycia frowned at the two drawings. "Yours are the same. Basically."

"They're not the same," Charles said. "Mine has the wall, the chloroplasts, and the big water bubble thing."

"Vacuole," Martin said, in the tone of someone who had spelled it wrong on a quiz and never forgiven himself.

Alycia tapped the animal cell drawing with one finger. "Then why does the animal one have this extra bit? Two little rods, right here. My drawing has them too. Did we inherit them from the same board notes, or did you just not copy fast enough?"

Charles stared at the tiny rods. He had copied fast, thank you. He'd checked. Which meant the rods were in the animal cell and not in the plant cell, and that was a real difference, not a rushed one. "That's an inference," he said slowly. "The rods are only in animals. I'm inferring."

"You're showing off," said Martin.

"I'm inferring." Charles flipped the worksheet over and wrote it down. Alycia peered at the board notes on her own sheet and found the label. "Centrioles," she read. "Animal cells have them. And most plant cells don't."

"So plants just divide without them," Charles said. "Show-offs."

Ms. Khoury handed him a bent tomato stake. "Inferring is fine," she said. "Hammering is better."

Charles hammered, worksheet pinned under a rock beside him, centrioles circled twice for good measure.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: One of the first written guides to online manners, 'Netiquette Guidelines', was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855.
story:
The bus smelled like wet sneakers and oranges, and Lincoln had his phone balanced on his knee, glaring at the class group chat. Someone had typed twenty-seven walrus emojis at five in the morning. Then someone else had answered with a foghorn sound. Then the chat had somehow become a debate about whether Mr. Grant's mustache counted as agriculture, because Hope had started it and she could make anything sound scientific.

"We need rules," Lincoln said.

Mikaella, two seats over, leaned across the aisle. "You can't just invent rules. People will assume you're being bossy, and then they'll send more walruses out of spite."

"That's exactly why I have to find out if official rules already exist. Like, real ones. Written down somewhere."

He searched, scrolling while the bus lurched around the corner by the farm stand. He typed "official online manners" and then, after another lurch, "old rules for chatting." What came up surprised him: a document called RFC 1855. "Listen to this," he said. "One of the first written guides to online manners, 'Netiquette Guidelines', was published in 1995."

"Netiquette," Mikaella repeated. "That's actually a word?"

"That's what it was called." He skimmed further. The old guide said things like don't shout in capitals, and think about how messages sound without a face attached. Lincoln had a theory forming: the walrus problem wasn't really about walruses. It was that in the group chat, everybody talked like they were alone in their bedrooms, which they were, instead of like they were on the bus together, where you could see people wince.

He tested it. He typed a message out loud first, in his normal voice, then changed the capitals to lowercase before sending.

NEW RULE, the message began, then his thumbs deleted it and started over. "New rule," it read instead. "Before you send something at 5 a.m., say it out loud like we're all sitting behind you. Also, the chat goes quiet after nine at night. Vote yes or send one walrus."

One walrus appeared within seconds, from Hope.

"That's a no," Lincoln said.

"That's a yes with an attitude," said Mikaella. "Significant difference."
